### C. elegans stains

C. elegans strains were maintained at 20 °C on NGM plates seeded with OP50 E. coli according to standard conditions unless otherwise stated (Brenner, 1974). All strains used in this project are listed in Supplementary file 1.

### CRISPR-mediated strain construction

For nrde-3(cmp324[HK-AA]), enri-1(cmp328), enri-2(cmp318), and rde-3/mut-2(cmp337), we used an oligo repair template and RNA guide. For enri-1(cmp320[enri-1::mCherry::2xHA]), we used an RNA guide and PCR amplified repair template (Supplementary file 2). For injections using a single gene-specific crRNA, the injection mix included 0.25  μg/μl Cas9 protein (IDT), 100  ng/μl tracrRNA (IDT), 14  ng/μl dpy-10 crRNA, 42  ng/μl gene-specific crRNA, and 110  ng/μl of the oligo repair template. For injections using two gene-specific crRNAs, the injection mix included 0.25  μg/μl Cas9 protein (IDT), 100  ng/μl tracrRNA (IDT), 14  ng/μl dpy-10 crRNA, 21  ng/μl each gene-specific crRNA, and 110  ng/μl of each repair template.

The following strains were used for injection: enri-2(cmp318) and enri-1(cmp320[enri-1::mCherry::2xHA]) into wild-type N2 strain. nrde-3(cmp324[HK-AA]) and enri-1(cmp328) into JMC237: nrde-3(tor131[GFP::3xFLAG::nrde-3]) X. rde-3/mut-2(cmp337) into USC1615: ego-1(cmp317[ego-1::degron]) I; ieSi38 [Psun-1::TIR1::mRuby::sun-1 3’ UTR] IV; nrde-3(tor131[GFP::3xFLAG::nrde-3]) X. Following injection, F1 animals with the Rol phenotype were isolated and genotyped by PCR to identify heterozygous animals with the mutations of interest, then F2 animals were further singled out to identify homozygous mutant animals.

### RNAi assays

For RNAi experiment, control L4440 and lgg-1 RNAi E. coli clones were sequenced verified and cultured at 37 °C for 16 hours, then RNAi bacteria were seeded on fresh RNAi plates. Two L4 animals were transferred to seeded RNAi plates and raised at 20 °C. When the progenies of the L4 animals turn into young adults (about 4 days), the embryos of young adult animals were imaged to assess somatic granule expression.

### Immunofluorescence imaging and quantification

For immunofluorescence, C. elegans were dissected in egg buffer containing 0.1% Tween-20 and fixed in 1% formaldehyde in egg buffer as described (Phillips et al., 2009). Samples were immunostained with anti-RNA Polymerase II CTD (phosphoSer2) at 1:500 (Abcam ab5095). The secondary antibody, anti-Rabbit IgG AlexaFluor 555 was used at 1:1000 (Thermo Fisher A21429). Animals were dissected at the adult stage (24  h post L4). Imaging was performed on a DeltaVision Elite microscope (GE Healthcare) using a 60 x N.A. 1.42 oil-immersion objective, data stacks were collected and deconvolution was performed using the SoftWoRx package. 25 optical sections, for a total 12.5 µm sample thickness, are presented as a maximum intensity projection. PSer2 signal intensity was calculated in ImageJ (version 1.53 a) using a minimum of 10 individual adult gonads.

### Live imaging

Live imaging of C. elegans embryos was performed in M9 buffer. Young embryos were obtained by dissecting gravid adult C. elegans, and old embryos were obtained by manually picking embryos laid on the NGM plate. Live imaging of C. elegans adult germline was performed in M9 buffer containing sodium azide to prevent movement. Day-one-adult C. elegans were obtained by manually picking L4s and leaving L4s at 20 °C for about 24 hr. Imaging was performed on a DeltaVision Elite microscope (GE Healthcare) using a 60 x N.A. 1.42 oil-immersion objective. Images were pseudocolored using Adobe Photoshop.

### Granule number quantification

Granule number quantification was performed in FIJI/ImageJ2 (version 2.9.0). At least 10 embryos were imaged on a DeltaVision Elite microscope with 37 optical sections of a total 22.20 µm sample thickness from the bottom of the sample. Images were deconvolved to eliminate backgrounds. Z stacks were opened using the 3D object counter plugin for FIJI, and the granule counting threshold for each image was manually adjusted to obtain the least background and most granules.

### Colocalization analysis

Quantitative colocalization analysis between different granules was performed in FIJI/ImageJ2 (version 2.9.0) using the Coloc2 package and 100 cell staged embryos imaged on a DeltaVision Elite microscope. At least 3 granules from each embryo, and at least 4 individual embryos for a total of at least 20 granules were used to calculate Pearson’s R value.

### Western blot

Synchronized adult C. elegans were harvested (∼72 hours at 20 °C after L1 arrest) and 200 adults were loaded per lane. Proteins were resolved on 4–12% Bis-Tris polyacrylamide gels (Thermo Fisher, NW04122BOX), transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Thermo Fisher, LC2001), and probed with rat anti-HA-peroxidase 1:1000 (Roche 12013819001), mouse anti-FLAG 1:1000 (Sigma, F1804), or mouse anti-actin 1:10,000 (Abcam ab3280). Secondary HRP antibodies were purchased from Thermo Fisher. Unedited western blots are provided in the Source Data File.

### Small RNA library preparation and sequencing

For C. elegans embryo staging and collection, synchronized arrested L1s were grown on enriched peptone plates at 17 °C until the young adult stage. Adult C. elegans stage was monitored carefully under DeltaVision microscope by live imaging. For early embryo collection (≤ 100 cell), adult animals were washed off from plates with H2O and bleached as soon as the first animals had 1–4 eggs (around 68–70 hours depending on the strain and the incubator temperature). For late embryo collection (≥ 300 cell), adult animals were washed off from plates with H2O and bleached when about half of the worms had 1~6 eggs (around 70–72 hours depending on the strain and the incubator temperature). After bleaching, embryos were washed twice with M9 buffer, and filtered through 40 µm cell strainers (Fisherbrand Sterile Cell Strainers, 40 µm) twice to clear the residual worm body. To reach ≥ 300 cell stage for late embryo collection, embryos were additionally incubated in M9 buffer at 20 °C for 4.5 hr. Then embryos were washed once with IP buffer (50 mM Tris-Cl pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 0.1% Nonidet P40 substitute) containing Protease Inhibitor (Thermo Fisher A32965). Embryos were kept on ice during washes to prevent further development. 500,000 embryos were collected for each replicate. Following washes, embryos were flash-frozen by placing tubes in a container with ethanol and dry ice. A small aliquot of embryos was examined on the Deltavision microscope to confirm the developmental stage immediately before freezing. Frozen embryos were stored at –80 °C until immunoprecipitation.

For immunoprecipitation followed by small RNA sequencing in embryos, ∼500,000 synchronized embryos were sonicated with Fisher Sonifier 550 with a microtip (15 s on, 45 s off, 10% power, total 2 min on time). After sonication, insoluble particulate was removed by centrifugation at 21,000 × g for 30 min. Immunoprecipitation was performed using anti-FLAG Affinity Matrix (Sigma Aldrich, A2220). NRDE-3-bound RNAs were isolated using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher, 15596018), followed by chloroform extraction and isopropanol precipitation. Small RNAs (18–30-nt) were size selected on homemade 10% Urea-polyacrylamide gels from total RNA samples. Small RNAs were treated with 5’ RNA polyphosphatase (Epicenter RP8092H) and ligated to 3’ pre-adenylated adapters with Truncated T4 RNA ligase (NEB M0373L). Small RNAs were then hybridized to the reverse transcription primer, ligated to the 5’ adapter with T4 RNA ligase (NEB M0204L), and reverse transcribed with Superscript III (Thermo Fisher 18080–051). Small RNA libraries were amplified using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA polymerase (NEB M0491L) and size selected on a homemade 10% polyacrylamide gel. Library concentration was determined using the Qubit 1 X dsDNA HS Assay kit (Thermo Fisher Q33231) and quality was assessed using the Agilent BioAnalyzer. Libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq2000 (SE 75 bp reads) platform. Primer sequences are available in Supplementary file 2. Differentially expressed gene lists and gene lists used in this paper can be found in Supplementary file 3. Sequencing library statistics summary can be found in Supplementary file 4.

### Bioinformatic analysis

For small RNA libraries, sequences were parsed from adapters and quality filtered using FASTX-Toolkit (version 0.0.13) (Hannon, 2010). Filtered reads were mapped to the C. elegans genome, WS258, using Bowtie2 (version 2.5.0) (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012). Mapped reads were assigned to genomic features using featureCounts which is part of the Subread package (version 2.0.1) (Liao et al., 2014). Differential expression analysis was performed using edgeR (3.40.2) (Robinson et al., 2010). To define gene lists from IP experiments, a twofold-change cutoff, an edgeR adjusted p-value of ≤0.05, and at least 10 RPM in the IP libraries were required to identify genes with significant changes in small RNA levels.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102226.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102226.3.sa1)

Summary:

Chen and Phillips describe the dynamic appearance of cytoplasmic granules during embryogenesis analogous to SIMR germ granules, and distinct from CSR-1-containing granules, in the C. elegans germline. They show that the nuclear Argonaute NRDE-3, when mutated to abrogate small RNA binding, or in specific genetic mutants, partially colocalizes to these granules along with other RNAi factors, such as SIMR-1, ENRI-2, RDE-3, and RRF-1. Furthermore, NRDE-3 RIP-seq analysis in early vs. late embryos is used to conclude that NRDE-3 binds CSR-1-dependent 22G RNAs in early embryos and ERGO-1-dependent 22G RNAs in late embryos. These data lead to their model that NRDE-3 undergoes small RNA substrate ‘switching’ that occurs in these embryonic SIMR granules and functions to silence two distinct sets of target transcripts - maternal, CSR-1 targeted mRNAs in early embryos and duplicated genes and repeat elements in late embryos.

Strengths:

The identification and function of small RNA-related granules during embryogenesis is a poorly understood area and this study will provide the impetus for future studies on the identification and potential functional compartmentalization of small RNA pathways and machinery during embryogenesis.

Weaknesses:

(1) The authors acknowledge the following issue that loss of SIMR granules have no significant impact on NRDE-3 small RNA loading weakens the functional relevance of these structures. However, this point is clearly discussed and, as they note in their Discussion, it is entirely possible that these embryonic granules may be ‘incidental condensates.’

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102226.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102226.3.sa2)

Summary:

NRDE-3 is a nuclear WAGO-clade Argonaute that, in somatic cells, binds small RNAs amplified in response to the ERGO-class 26G RNAs that target repetitive sequences. This manuscript reports that, in the germline and early embryos, NRDE-3 interacts with a different set of small RNAs that target mRNAs. This class of small RNAs were previously shown to bind to a different WAGO-clade Argonaute called CSR-1, which is cytoplasmic unlike nuclear NRDE-3. The switch in NRDE-3 specificity parallels recent findings in Ascaris where the Ascaris NRDE homolog was shown to switch from sRNAs that target repetitive sequences to CSR-class sRNAs that target mRNAs.

The manuscript also correlates the change in NRDE-3 specificity with the appearance in embryos of cytoplasmic condensates that accumulate SIMR-1, a scaffolding protein that the authors previously implicated in sRNA loading for a different nuclear Argonaute HRDE-1. By analogy, and through a set of corelative evidence, the authors argue that SIMR foci arise in embryogenesis to facilitate the change in NRDE-3 small RNA repertoire. The paper presents lots of data that beautifully documents the appearance and composition of the embryonic SIMR-1 foci, including evidence that a mutated NRDE-3 that cannot bind sRNAs accumulate in SIMR-1 foci in SIMR-1-dependent fashion.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E showing NRDE-3(HK-AA) localization in the germline.

claims.claim: In eri-1 and rde-3 mutants, NRDE-3 localizes to the nucleus in early embryos while NRDE-3(HK-AA) localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Specifically, in eri-1 and rde-3 mutants, NRDE-3 localizes to the nucleus in early embryos while NRDE-3(HK-AA) localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A comparing NRDE-3 localization in different mutant backgrounds.

claims.claim: In the Z2 and Z3 primordial germ cells of late embryos, NRDE-3 is still found in the nucleus in eri-1 and rde-3 mutants.
claims.source: Similarly, in the Z2 and Z3 primordial germ cells of late embryos, NRDE-3 is still found in the nucleus in eri-1 and rde-3 mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A showing NRDE-3 nuclear localization in primordial germ cells of mutant embryos.

claims.claim: NRDE-3 localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm in the somatic cells of late embryos in eri-1, rde-3, and nrde-3(HK-AA) mutants.
claims.source: In contrast, NRDE-3 localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm in the somatic cells of late embryos of all three mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A showing NRDE-3 localization in somatic cells of late embryos in different mutant backgrounds.

claims.claim: There may be a fundamental difference in the small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early compared to late embryos.
claims.source: This result suggests that there may be a fundamental difference in the small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early compared to late embryos, and that the small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early embryos are produced independently of ERI-1 and RDE-3.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NRDE-3 remains nuclear in early embryos of eri-1 and rde-3 mutants but becomes cytoplasmic in late embryos.

claims.claim: The small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early embryos are produced independently of ERI-1 and RDE-3.
claims.source: This result suggests that there may be a fundamental difference in the small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early compared to late embryos, and that the small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 in early embryos are produced independently of ERI-1 and RDE-3.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that NRDE-3 remains nuclear in early embryos of eri-1 and rde-3 mutants.

claims.claim: NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules disappear completely and NRDE-3(HK-AA) is found exclusively in the cytoplasm in all cells across all embryonic stages in simr-1 and enri-2 mutants.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules disappear completely and NRDE-3(HK-AA) is instead found exclusively in the cytoplasm in all cells across all embryonic stages (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3A showing NRDE-3(HK-AA) localization in simr-1 and enri-2 mutants.

claims.claim: In a simr-1; eri-1 double mutant, NRDE-3 granules are absent though NRDE-3 remains in the nucleus in early embryos.
claims.source: Similarly, in a simr-1; eri-1 double mutant, NRDE-3 granules are absent though NRDE-3 remains in the nucleus in early embryos (Figure 3A), similar to NRDE-3 expression in the eri-1 single mutant (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3A showing NRDE-3 localization in the simr-1; eri-1 double mutant.

claims.claim: Neither wild-type NRDE-3 nor NRDE-3(HK-AA) protein levels are affected by loss of simr-1.
claims.source: However, neither wild-type NRDE-3 nor NRDE-3(HK-AA) protein levels are affected by loss of simr-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that loss of granule localization in nrde-3(HK-AA); simr-1 is not due to reduced NRDE-3 protein expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing NRDE-3 protein levels in simr-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Both SIMR-1 and ENRI-2 are required for the recruitment of NRDE-3 to cytoplasmic granules.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that both SIMR-1 and ENRI-2 are required for the recruitment of NRDE-3 to cytoplasmic granules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3A showing loss of NRDE-3 granule localization in simr-1 and enri-2 mutants.

claims.claim: ENRI-2 granules are lost in the simr-1 mutant.
claims.source: We found that ENRI-2 granules are lost in the simr-1 mutant, while SIMR-1 granules are still present in the enri-2 mutant, indicating that SIMR-1 functions upstream of ENRI-2 for granule assembly (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3B showing ENRI-2 localization in the simr-1 mutant.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 granules are still present in the enri-2 mutant.
claims.source: We found that ENRI-2 granules are lost in the simr-1 mutant, while SIMR-1 granules are still present in the enri-2 mutant, indicating that SIMR-1 functions upstream of ENRI-2 for granule assembly (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3B showing SIMR-1 localization in the enri-2 mutant.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 functions upstream of ENRI-2 for granule assembly.
claims.source: We found that ENRI-2 granules are lost in the simr-1 mutant, while SIMR-1 granules are still present in the enri-2 mutant, indicating that SIMR-1 functions upstream of ENRI-2 for granule assembly (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ENRI-2 requires SIMR-1 for granule localization but SIMR-1 does not require ENRI-2.

claims.claim: NRDE-3 association with cytoplasmic granules is not disrupted in an enri-1 mutant.
claims.source: To further assess whether ENRI-1 plays a role in the accumulation of unloaded NRDE-3 in cytoplasmic granules, we introduced an enri-1 mutant into the GFP-tagged NRDE-3(HK-AA) strain and found that NRDE-3 association with cytoplasmic granules was not disrupted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing NRDE-3(HK-AA) granule localization in the enri-1 mutant.

claims.claim: NRDE-3(HK-AA) granule association in the enri-1; enri-2 double mutant is fully cytoplasmic, indistinguishable from the enri-2 single mutant.
claims.source: We further examined NRDE-3(HK-AA) granule association in the enri-1; enri-2 double mutant and found it to be fully cytoplasmic, indistinguishable from the enri-2 single mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing NRDE-3(HK-AA) localization in the enri-1; enri-2 double mutant.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 and ENRI-2, but not ENRI-1, recruit unloaded NRDE-3 to cytoplasmic granules, with SIMR-1 also acting to recruit ENRI-2.
claims.source: Therefore, we excluded ENRI-1 from further investigation, and conclude that SIMR-1 and ENRI-2, but not ENRI-1, recruit unloaded NRDE-3 to cytoplasmic granules, with SIMR-1 also acting to recruit ENRI-2.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that SIMR-1 and ENRI-2 are required for NRDE-3 granule localization, SIMR-1 is required for ENRI-2 granule localization, and ENRI-1 is not required for NRDE-3 granule localization.

claims.claim: CGH-1 does not colocalize with SIMR-1 in embryos.
claims.source: To examine if the SIMR-1 cytoplasmic granules are P bodies, we examined the localization of SIMR-1 and CGH-1, a core P body component, using a strain expressing GFP-tagged SIMR-1 and mCherry-tagged CGH-1 (Du et al., 2023). We found that CGH-1 does not colocalize with SIMR-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing lack of colocalization between SIMR-1 and CGH-1, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: CGH-1 does not colocalize with NRDE-3 cytoplasmic granules in the eri-1 mutant.
claims.source: CGH-1 also does not colocalize with NRDE-3 cytoplasmic granules in the eri-1 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B showing lack of colocalization between NRDE-3 and CGH-1 in the eri-1 mutant.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic SIMR granules found in embryos are not P bodies.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the cytoplasmic SIMR granules found in embryos are not P bodies.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SIMR-1 and NRDE-3 do not colocalize with the P body marker CGH-1.

claims.claim: RSD-2 does not localize to granules in embryos.
claims.source: However, we did not observe any granule localization for RSD-2 and HRDE-2 in embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing RSD-2 localization in embryos.

claims.claim: HRDE-2 does not localize to granules in embryos.
claims.source: However, we did not observe any granule localization for RSD-2 and HRDE-2 in embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D showing HRDE-2 localization in embryos.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 cytoplasmic granules are not affected by the loss of hrde-2.
claims.source: In addition, SIMR-1 cytoplasmic granules were not affected by the loss of hrde-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E showing SIMR-1 granule localization in the hrde-2 mutant.

claims.claim: Embryonic SIMR granules and the SIMR compartment of germ granules are distinct, each containing a unique set of proteins.
claims.source: These results suggest that HRDE-2 and RSD-2 do not function together with SIMR-1, ENRI-2, and NRDE-3 in embryonic granules and indicate that embryonic SIMR granules and the SIMR compartment of germ granules are distinct, each containing a unique set of proteins.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that HRDE-2 and RSD-2, which localize to germline SIMR foci, do not localize to embryonic SIMR granules.

claims.claim: RDE-12 does not colocalize with SIMR-1 in embryos.
claims.source: We next assessed the localization of mCherry-tagged SIMR-1 relative to GFP-tagged RDE-12 and found that they do not colocalize (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F showing lack of colocalization between SIMR-1 and RDE-12.

claims.claim: RSD-6 localizes to granules in somatic cells of embryos but does not colocalize with SIMR-1.
claims.source: We examined the expression of GFP-tagged RSD-6 in embryos and did observe RSD-6 at granules in somatic cells, while no colocalization with mCherry-tagged SIMR-1 could be detected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G showing RSD-6 and SIMR-1 localization in embryos.

claims.claim: ZNFX-1 localizes to cytoplasmic granules in the somatic cells of embryos but does not colocalize with SIMR-1.
claims.source: The RNAi-inheritance factor and defining member of the Z compartment of the germ granule, ZNFX-1, has also been observed in cytoplasmic granules in the somatic cells of embryos (Wan et al., 2018; Ouyang et al., 2019), however these somatic ZNFX-1 granules also fail to colocalize with SIMR-1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H showing lack of colocalization between SIMR-1 and ZNFX-1, with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 does not colocalize with peri-centrosomal foci marked by tubulin.
claims.source: Finally, we compared SIMR-1 localization to peri-centrosomal foci marked tubulin, based on a recent report that NRDE-3 accumulates at these foci (Jin et al., 2024), but we did not observe any colocalization between SIMR-1 and tubulin in a wild-type background (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I showing lack of colocalization between SIMR-1 and tubulin, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 fails to localize to any previously characterized embryonic granules.
claims.source: Altogether, we found that SIMR-1 fails to localize to any previously characterized embryonic granules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined observations that SIMR-1 does not colocalize with CGH-1, RDE-12, RSD-6, ZNFX-1, or tubulin.

claims.claim: RDE-3/MUT-2 is prominently localized to cytoplasmic granules in embryos that colocalize with SIMR-1.
claims.source: We first examined Mutator foci component RDE-3/MUT-2, a poly(UG) polymerase required for WAGO-class 22G-RNA production (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B; Phillips et al., 2012; Shukla et al., 2020) and found that GFP-tagged RDE-3 is prominently localized to cytoplasmic granules in embryos that colocalize with SIMR-1 (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4A and colocalization analysis in Figure 4B, with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: RRF-1 colocalizes with SIMR-1 in somatic granules.
claims.source: As we predicted, RRF-1 also colocalizes with SIMR-1 in somatic granules (Figure 4B–C), and it fails to localize to somatic granules in the simr-1 mutant (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4C and colocalization analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: RRF-1 fails to localize to somatic granules in the simr-1 mutant.
claims.source: As we predicted, RRF-1 also colocalizes with SIMR-1 in somatic granules (Figure 4B–C), and it fails to localize to somatic granules in the simr-1 mutant (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4D showing RRF-1 localization in the simr-1 mutant.

claims.claim: MUT-16 localizes to cytoplasmic granules in the embryonic somatic cells.
claims.source: We found that MUT-16 can be observed in cytoplasmic granules in the embryonic somatic cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), similar to what has been observed in a previous study (Ouyang et al., 2019), and both SIMR-1 and RDE-3 fail to assemble into cytoplasmic granules in the mut-16 mutant (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J showing MUT-16 localization in embryos, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Both SIMR-1 and RDE-3 fail to assemble into cytoplasmic granules in the mut-16 mutant.
claims.source: We found that MUT-16 can be observed in cytoplasmic granules in the embryonic somatic cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), similar to what has been observed in a previous study (Ouyang et al., 2019), and both SIMR-1 and RDE-3 fail to assemble into cytoplasmic granules in the mut-16 mutant (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K showing SIMR-1 and RDE-3 localization in the mut-16 mutant.

claims.claim: The germ granule association of SIMR-1 is unaffected in the mut-16 mutant, as SIMR-1 still localizes to germ granules at comma stage embryos and in the adult germline.
claims.source: Notably, the germ granule association of SIMR-1 is unaffected, as SIMR-1 still localizes to germ granules at comma stage embryos and in the adult germline (Figure 4E; Manage et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4E showing SIMR-1 localization in germ granules of mut-16 mutant embryos, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: MUT-16 functions upstream of SIMR-1 and mediates the assembly of cytoplasmic granules in embryos.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that MUT-16 functions upstream of SIMR-1 and mediates the assembly of cytoplasmic granules in embryos.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that SIMR-1 and RDE-3 fail to form cytoplasmic granules in the mut-16 mutant.

claims.claim: In a mut-16 mutant where SIMR-1 association with cytoplasmic granules is lost in the somatic cells, SIMR-1 instead associates with mitotic spindles.
claims.source: It is curious to note that, in a mut-16 mutant where SIMR-1 association with cytoplasmic granules is lost in the somatic cells, SIMR-1 instead associates with mitotic spindles (Figure 4E), similar to the localization observed for NRDE-3 in embryos (Jin et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4E showing SIMR-1 spindle localization in the mut-16 mutant, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The SIMR granules found in the somatic cells of early embryos contain the biogenesis machinery for WAGO-class 22G-RNAs, including RDE-3 and RRF-1, and depend on the scaffolding protein MUT-16 for assembly.
claims.source: To conclude, we have shown that the SIMR granules found in the somatic cells of early embryos contain the biogenesis machinery for WAGO-class 22G-RNAs, including RDE-3 and RRF-1, and depend on the scaffolding protein MUT-16 for assembly (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined observations that RDE-3 and RRF-1 colocalize with SIMR-1, and that SIMR-1 and RDE-3 require MUT-16 for granule assembly.

claims.claim: The differential requirement for MUT-16 on the assembly of somatic and germline SIMR granules highlights a key difference between these two compartments, which have some parallel functions but distinct composition.
claims.source: The differential requirement for MUT-16 on the assembly of somatic and germline SIMR granules highlights a key difference between these two compartments, which have some parallel functions but distinct composition.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that MUT-16 is required for somatic SIMR granule assembly but not germline SIMR foci assembly.

claims.claim: CSR-1 forms prominent cytoplasmic granules in embryos visible prior to the 4 cell stage and present through 100 cell stage embryos, but disappear by the 200 cell stage, at which point only germ granule localization is visible.
claims.source: Using a GFP-tagged CSR-1 strain we constructed previously (Nguyen and Phillips, 2021), we confirmed that CSR-1 forms prominent cytoplasmic granules in embryos visible prior to the 4 cell stage and present through 100 cell stage embryos, but disappear by the 200 cell stage, at which point only germ granule localization is visible (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4F showing CSR-1 localization across embryonic development, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: CSR granules are more abundant than the SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules and differ in the timing of their appearance and disappearance relative to SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules.
claims.source: Quantification of the total number of 'CSR granules' per embryo across development shows that the CSR granules are more abundant than the SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules and differ in the timing of their appearance and disappearance relative to SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules (Figures 1C, 2C and 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 4G compared to Figures 1C and 2C showing granule dynamics across embryonic development.

claims.claim: CSR granules appear earlier and peak at the 28 cell stage, while SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules appear between 8- and 28 cell stages and peak at the 100 cell stage.
claims.source: Specifically, CSR granules appear earlier and peak at the 28 cell stage, while SIMR-1 and NRDE-3(HK-AA) granules appear between 8- and 28 cell stages and peak at the 100 cell stage (Figures 1C, 2C and 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figures 1C, 2C, and 4G showing the temporal dynamics of different granule types.

claims.claim: EGO-1 colocalizes with CSR-1 in the somatic CSR granules.
claims.source: The small RNAs bound by CSR-1 are synthesized by the RdRP, EGO-1, so we next assessed the localization of EGO-1 in early embryos. We found that EGO-1 colocalizes with CSR-1 in the somatic CSR granules (Figure 4B and H) and neither CSR-1 nor EGO-1 fully colocalizes with SIMR-1, although we occasionally observed adjacent localization between SIMR-1 and CSR-1 (Figure 4B and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4H and colocalization analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Neither CSR-1 nor EGO-1 fully colocalizes with SIMR-1, although occasionally adjacent localization between SIMR-1 and CSR-1 is observed.
claims.source: We found that EGO-1 colocalizes with CSR-1 in the somatic CSR granules (Figure 4B and H) and neither CSR-1 nor EGO-1 fully colocalizes with SIMR-1, although we occasionally observed adjacent localization between SIMR-1 and CSR-1 (Figure 4B and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1L, and colocalization analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: EGO-1 localizes to cytoplasmic granules in the absence of SIMR-1.
claims.source: Lastly, unlike RRF-1 which requires SIMR-1 to localize to embryonic foci, EGO-1 localizes to cytoplasmic granules in the absence of SIMR-1 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 4D showing EGO-1 localization in the simr-1 mutant.

claims.claim: The RdRPs, RRF-1 and EGO-1, localize to different cytoplasmic granules in the somatic cells of C. elegans embryos, where they colocalize with Argonaute proteins, NRDE-3 and CSR-1, respectively.
claims.source: Together, our results show that the RdRPs, RRF-1 and EGO-1, localize to different cytoplasmic granules in the somatic cells of C. elegans embryos, where they colocalize with Argonaute proteins, NRDE-3 and CSR-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined observations that RRF-1 colocalizes with SIMR-1 and unloaded NRDE-3, while EGO-1 colocalizes with CSR-1.

claims.claim: WAGO-class and CSR-class 22G-RNA biogenesis and loading are compartmentalized into cytoplasmic granules, differing from one another both spatially and temporally, in the somatic cells of early embryos.
claims.source: Thus, we postulate that WAGO-class and CSR-class 22G-RNA biogenesis and loading are compartmentalized into cytoplasmic granules, differing from one another both spatially and temporally, in the somatic cells of early embryos (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on the observation that RRF-1 and EGO-1 localize to different granules with different temporal dynamics.

claims.claim: Autophagic degradation is one mechanism by which P granules are removed from somatic blastomeres.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that autophagic degradation is one mechanism by which P granules are removed from somatic blastomeres (Zhang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on P granule degradation.

claims.claim: In the absence of the autophagy protein LGG-1, the core P granule proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 are ectopically expressed in somatic foci during mid to late embryogenesis.
claims.source: In the absence of the autophagy protein LGG-1, the C. elegans ortholog of S. cerevisiae Atg8, the core P granule proteins PGL-1 and PGL-3 are ectopically expressed in somatic foci during mid to late embryogenesis (Zhang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on P granule degradation.

claims.claim: RNAi of lgg-1 leads to ectopic expression of PGL-1 in cytoplasmic foci of the somatic cells at mid (100 cell) and late (comma) embryonic stages, while its germ granule localization remains unaffected.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Zhang et al., 2009), RNAi of lgg-1 leads to ectopic expression of PGL-1 in cytoplasmic foci of the somatic cells at mid (100 cell) and late (comma) embryonic stages, while its germ granule localization remains unaffected (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5A showing PGL-1 localization following lgg-1 RNAi, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The number of somatic SIMR granules at the 100 cell stage increases by approximately 2-fold in lgg-1 RNAi-treated embryos compared to control.
claims.source: Similarly, we found that the number of somatic SIMR granules at the 100 cell stage increases by approximately 2-fold in lgg-1 RNAi-treated embryos compared to control (L4440) (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5A and quantification in Figure 5B showing SIMR-1 granule numbers following lgg-1 RNAi.

claims.claim: In the comma stage, somatic SIMR granules remain in the soma in lgg-1 RNAi-treated embryos, whereas SIMR granules are cleared from the somatic cells and restricted to germ cells in control RNAi-treated embryos.
claims.source: Further, in the comma stage, somatic SIMR granules remain in the soma in lgg-1 RNAi-treated embryos, whereas SIMR granules are cleared from the somatic cells and restricted to germ cells in control (L4440) RNAi-treated embryos (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5A showing SIMR-1 localization in comma stage embryos following lgg-1 RNAi.

claims.claim: ENRI-2, RDE-3, RRF-1, and unloaded NRDE-3 exhibit ectopic expression in the somatic cells of comma-stage embryos following lgg-1 RNAi and continue to colocalize with SIMR-1.
claims.source: Examination of other somatic SIMR granule-associated proteins, including ENRI-2, RDE-3, and RRF-1, and unloaded NRDE-3 revealed that they also exhibit ectopic expression in the somatic cells of comma-stage embryos and continue to colocalize with SIMR-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and colocalization analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The removal of SIMR granules from somatic cells during mid and late embryogenesis is regulated by autophagy, similar to the role of autophagy in the degradation of P granules from early somatic blastomeres.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the removal of SIMR granules from somatic cells during mid and late embryogenesis is regulated by autophagy, similar to the role of autophagy in the degradation of P granules form early somatic blastomeres.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that lgg-1 RNAi leads to persistence of SIMR granules in somatic cells, similar to what is observed for P granules.

claims.claim: CSR-1 and ZNFX-1 show increased numbers of somatic granules in 100 cell and comma stage embryos following parental treatment with lgg-1 RNAi compared to control.
claims.source: Similar to PGL-1 and SIMR-1, CSR-1 and ZNFX-1 show increased numbers of somatic granules in 100 cell and comma stage embryos following parental treatment with lgg-1 RNAi compared to control (L4440) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5C showing CSR-1 and ZNFX-1 localization following lgg-1 RNAi.

claims.claim: In 100 cell stage embryos following lgg-1 RNAi treatment, PGL-1, SIMR-1, ZNFX-1, and CSR-1 display a variety of configurations relative to one another, including granules composed of individual protein, multiple proteins adjacent to one another, and large aggregates composed of multiple proteins.
claims.source: Interestingly, these proteins display a variety of configurations relative to one another, distinct from their typical organization in the germline (Uebel et al., 2023). These configurations included granules composed of individual protein, multiple proteins adjacent to one another, and large aggregates composed of multiple proteins (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 5D showing the spatial organization of multiple granule proteins following lgg-1 RNAi, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The autophagy pathway is utilized to regulate the spatial-temporal expression of many embryonic granule-associated proteins, including proteins found in P, Z, SIMR, and CSR granules.
claims.source: Overall, our findings demonstrate that the autophagy pathway is utilized to regulate the spatial-temporal expression of many embryonic granule-associated proteins, including proteins found in P, Z, SIMR, and CSR granules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined observations that lgg-1 RNAi leads to persistence of PGL-1, SIMR-1, ZNFX-1, and CSR-1 in somatic cells.

claims.claim: P, Z, SIMR, and CSR granules are not all removed at the same developmental timepoint.
claims.source: Further, it is worth noting that P, Z, SIMR, and CSR granules are not all removed at the same developmental timepoint (for example, Figures 1C and 4G), suggesting the presence of additional regulatory mechanisms controlling the timing of their degradation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figures 1C and 4G showing different temporal dynamics for different granule types.

claims.claim: In eri-1 and rde-3 mutants where 26G-RNA or WAGO-class 22G-RNA biogenesis are abolished, respectively, NRDE-3 remains localized to the nucleus in early embryos.
claims.source: Specifically, in eri-1 and rde-3 mutants where 26G-RNA or WAGO-class 22G-RNA biogenesis are abolished, respectively, NRDE-3 remains localized to the nucleus in early embryos (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A showing NRDE-3 nuclear localization in eri-1 and rde-3 mutants.

claims.claim: The small RNA binding-defective NRDE-3(HK-AA) is localized exclusively to the cytoplasm in early embryos, indicating that small RNA binding is critical for nuclear import at this stage.
claims.source: The small RNA binding-defective NRDE-3(HK-AA) is localized exclusively to the cytoplasm at the same time point, indicating that small RNA binding is critical for nuclear import at this stage (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data in Figure 2A showing NRDE-3(HK-AA) cytoplasmic localization in early embryos.

claims.claim: In early embryos, the majority of small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 are CSR-class 22G-RNAs, which become progressively less enriched as the animals develop into late embryos and then young adults.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that in early embryos, the majority of small RNAs bound by NRDE-3 are CSR-class 22G-RNAs, which become progressively less enriched as the animals develop into late embryos and then young adults (Figure 6B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6B-D comparing NRDE-3-bound small RNAs across developmental stages.

claims.claim: CSR-class 22G-RNAs are likely sufficient to promote nuclear entry of NRDE-3 in the early embryo.

claims.claim: In the eri-1 mutant, NRDE-3 shows a reduction in binding to ERGO-dependent small RNAs and an increase in binding to CSR-class small RNAs in late embryos.

claims.claim: In the simr-1 mutant, there is a significant increase of CSR-class 22G-RNA binding by NRDE-3 in late embryos.

claims.claim: In the enri-2 mutant, there is a modest but still significant increase of CSR-class 22G-RNA binding by NRDE-3 in late embryos.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B showing NRDE-3-bound small RNAs in the enri-2 mutant.

claims.claim: SIMR-1 and ENRI-2 are not required for the production of the ERGO-dependent small RNAs during embryogenesis, but may be required for an efficient switch from CSR-class to ERGO-dependent 22G-RNAs.

claims.claim: The genes targeted by NRDE-3 in early embryos substantially overlap with CSR-target genes in embryos and young adult animals.

We found that the genes targeted by NRDE-3 substantially overlap with CSR-target genes at both stages (Figure 7A; Quarato et al., 2021; Nguyen and Phillips, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 7A comparing NRDE-3 and CSR-1 target genes, with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The CSR-target genes with the highest abundance of CSR-1-bound small RNAs in embryos also have the highest abundance of NRDE-3-bound small RNAs.
claims.source: Furthermore, the CSR-target genes yielding the highest abundance of CSR-1-bound small RNAs in embryos also have the highest abundance of NRDE-3-bound small RNAs (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data in Figure 7B showing correlation between CSR-1 and NRDE-3-bound small RNA abundance.

claims.claim: CSR-target genes with highly abundant CSR-bound small RNAs are highly enriched by NRDE-3 only in embryos and not in young adults.
claims.source: These CSR-target genes with highly abundant CSR-bound small RNAs are highly enriched by NRDE-3 only in embryos and not in young adults (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A comparing NRDE-3-bound small RNAs in embryos and adults.

claims.claim: Both NRDE-3 and CSR-1 are heavily enriched for small RNAs derived from the 3' ends of CSR-target genes in embryos.
claims.source: Comparing NRDE-3-bound small RNAs from early embryos to a published dataset of CSR-1-bound small RNA from mixed-stage embryos, we found that both NRDE-3 and CSR-1 are heavily enriched for small RNAs derived from the 3' ends of CSR-target genes in embryos (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by density plot analysis in Figure 7C showing small RNA distribution along CSR-target genes.

claims.claim: In adult animals, CSR-1-bound 22G-RNAs are still enriched for small RNA derived from the 3' end of CSR-target genes, however there is additionally a much higher enrichment of small RNAs derived from the gene bodies compared to in embryos.
claims.source: Interestingly, in adult animals, CSR-1-bound 22G-RNAs are still enriched for small RNA derived from the 3' end of CSR-target genes, however there is additionally a much higher enrichment of small RNAs derived from the gene bodies compared to in embryos (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by density plot analysis in Figure 7C comparing small RNA distribution in embryos and adults.

claims.claim: Two types of CSR-class 22G-RNAs exist: those that depend on CSR-1 catalytic activity for their production and are derived primarily from target gene bodies, and those that are produced independently of CSR-1 catalytic activity and are derived primarily from target 3' UTRs.
claims.source: It has previously been proposed that two types of CSR-class 22G-RNAs exist, those that depend on CSR-1 catalytic activity for their production and are derived primarily from target gene bodies, and those that are produced independently of CSR-1 catalytic activity and are derived primarily from target 3' UTRs (Singh et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Both NRDE-3 and CSR-1 bind only the CSR-1 catalytic activity-independent type of CSR-class 22G-RNA in early embryos.
claims.source: Our data points to both NRDE-3 and CSR-1 binding only the latter, CSR-1 catalytic activity-independent, type of CSR-class 22G-RNA in early embryos.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both NRDE-3 and CSR-1 bind small RNAs derived primarily from 3' UTRs in embryos.

claims.claim: NRDE-3 does not show enrichment for small RNAs derived from the 3' ends of ERGO target genes in embryos, and rather the small RNAs are distributed more evenly across the gene bodies.
claims.source: In contrast, NRDE-3 does not show enrichment for small RNAs derived from the 3' ends of ERGO target genes in embryos, and rather the small RNAs are distributed more evenly across the gene bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by density plot analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing small RNA distribution along ERGO-target genes.

claims.claim: NRDE-3 preferentially binds to transcripts degraded early in embryogenesis.

claims.claim: The mRNAs targeted by NRDE-3 in young embryos, which correspond primarily to CSR-target mRNAs, decrease in expression across development.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA sequencing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D showing expression changes of NRDE-3 target genes across development.

claims.claim: The mRNAs targeted by NRDE-3 in young adults, corresponding primarily to ERGO-target mRNAs, increase in expression across development.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA sequencing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D showing expression changes of NRDE-3 target genes across development.

claims.claim: NRDE-3 binds to the same group of small RNAs as CSR-1 in early embryos.
claims.source: Together, these data reveal that NRDE-3 binds to the same group of small RNAs as CSR-1 in early embryos.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined observations that NRDE-3 and CSR-1 target overlapping genes, bind small RNAs with similar abundance patterns and 3' UTR enrichment, and target early-degraded transcripts.

claims.claim: The number of embryos laid by the csr-1::degron; gfp::nrde-3(HK-AA) double mutant was significantly lower compared to the csr-1::degron single mutant on 4 mM auxin plates.
